CHAPTER 1.1 · LEARNING AREA 1

CHAPTER 1.1 · LEARNING AREA 1 · AUGUST · SEPTEMBER

Circle and line, circumcircle and incircle

A bicycle rolls along the road. The tyre touches the ground in exactly one point. A line can miss a circle, touch it or cut it. You learn how to tell which from the distance. And for every triangle you find two special circles: one that passes through all three corners and one that touches all three sides.

8 LESSONS2 UNITS3 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • distinguish an external line, a tangent and a secant and recognise them by their distance from the centre
  • construct a tangent at a point on the circle
  • construct the circumcircle of a triangle with the perpendicular bisectors
  • construct the incircle of a triangle with the angle bisectors
  • predict where the circumcentre lies
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. What is its radius?

The radius is half the diameter: 5 cm.

What is the line called that cuts a line segment at right angles through its midpoint?

The perpendicular bisector. You know it from Year 6.

An angle of 70° is bisected. How big is each half?

70° ÷ 2 = 35°

A triangle has the angles 40° and 60°. How big is the third angle?

180° − 40° − 60° = 80°

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Circle and line

The tyre touches the road in exactly one point. A stick laid across the tyre meets it twice. And a bird flying over the wheel does not come close to it at all. What always matters is: how far is the line from the centre?

A circle $k$ with centre $M$ and radius $r$ consists of all the points that are at distance $r$ from $M$. The distance $d$ of the point $M$ from a line $g$ is the length of the perpendicular from $M$ to $g$. The perpendicular is the shortest connection; it is at right angles to $g$.

KEY POINT · CIRCLE AND LINE

A circle with radius $r$ and a line at distance $d$ from the centre:

$d > r$: external line. No point in common.

$d = r$: tangent. Exactly one point in common, the point of contact $B$. The tangent is perpendicular to the radius $\overline{MB}$.

$d < r$: secant. Two points of intersection. The line segment between them is called a chord. The longest chord is the diameter.

Where the names come from: tangent from the Latin tangere, to touch, secant from secare, to cut. In German an external line is called “Passante”, from the French passer, to pass by.

Never three points: A line contains at most two points that are exactly at distance $r$ from $M$, one on each side of the foot of the perpendicular.

INTERACTIVE · EXTERNAL LINE, TANGENT, SECANT
EXAMPLE 1 · CONSTRUCTING A TANGENT

Draw a circle with centre $M$ and $r = 2.5$ cm and a point $B$ on the circle. Construct the tangent at $B$.

1. Draw the radius $\overline{MB}$ and extend it beyond $B$.

2. At $B$, draw the perpendicular to this line, with a set square or with compasses and ruler.

The perpendicular at $B$ is the tangent.

EXAMPLE 2 · THREE LINES

A circle has a radius of 3 cm. The line $g$ is at a distance of 2 cm from the centre, $h$ at 3 cm, $i$ at 4.5 cm.

Compare $d$ with $r = 3$ cm each time: $2 < 3$, $3 = 3$, $4.5 > 3$.

$g$ is a secant, $h$ a tangent, $i$ an external line.

EXERCISES

Draw a circle with $r = 3$ cm. Draw an external line, a tangent and a secant. Measure the distance of each from the centre.

For the external line you measure more than 3 cm, for the tangent exactly 3 cm, for the secant less than 3 cm.

A circle has $r = 4$ cm. How does a line lie at a distance of a) 5 cm   b) 4 cm   c) 3.9 cm   d) 0 cm?

a) external line   b) tangent   c) secant   d) secant through $M$: the chord is a diameter, 8 cm long.

Draw a circle with $r = 2$ cm and a line $g$ at a distance of 4 cm from $M$. Draw all the tangents to the circle that are parallel to $g$. How far are they from $g$?

There are two such tangents, one on each side of the circle. One is 2 cm from $g$, the other 6 cm.

Draw a circle with $r = 3$ cm. Draw two tangents that intersect at a right angle. What kind of quadrilateral do the two radii to the points of contact form with the tangents?

A square with side length 3 cm: it has four right angles (two at the points of contact, one at the point of intersection, so the fourth at $M$ as well) and two adjacent sides of equal length, the radii.

A stick lies on a wheel and touches it at a point $B$. Explain why the radius $\overline{MB}$ is perpendicular to the stick.

The perpendicular from $M$ to the stick is the shortest connection. If $\overline{MB}$ were not perpendicular, there would be a point of the stick closer to $M$ than $r$. It would lie inside the wheel, and the stick would be a secant. So $\overline{MB}$ is the perpendicular.

TEST YOURSELF!

A circle has $r = 5$ cm, a line has the distance $d = 7$ cm. How many points do they have in common?

$d > r$: external line, no point.

A line is a tangent to a circle with $r = 2.5$ cm. How far is it from the centre?

For a tangent $d = r = 2.5$ cm.

How long is the longest chord of a circle with $r = 4$ cm?

The diameter: 8 cm.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Circumcircle and incircle

Back to the well: all the points that are the same distance from the houses $A$ and $B$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$. So the well must lie on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$ and on that of $\overline{BC}$. Where they intersect is its place.

In the same way, all the points that are the same distance from the two arms of an angle lie on its angle bisector. With it you find the centre of the biggest circle in the triangle.

KEY POINT · CIRCUMCIRCLE AND INCIRCLE

Circumcircle: The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle intersect in one point $U$. It is at the same distance $r$ from all three corners. The circle with centre $U$ and radius $r$ passes through $A$, $B$ and $C$.

$U$ lies inside an acute-angled triangle, at the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right-angled one and outside an obtuse-angled one.

Incircle: The three angle bisectors intersect in one point $I$. It is at the same distance $\varrho$ from all three sides. The circle with centre $I$ and radius $\varrho$ touches all three sides. $I$ always lies inside.

Two are enough: $U$ lies on the perpendicular bisectors of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BC}$, so $\overline{UA} = \overline{UB}$ and $\overline{UB} = \overline{UC}$. Then $\overline{UA} = \overline{UC}$ too, and $U$ lies on the third perpendicular bisector. Two are enough for the construction; the third is the check.

The radius of the incircle is found with the perpendicular from $I$ to one side. Its foot is the point of contact.

INTERACTIVE · THE TWO CIRCLES OF A TRIANGLE
EXAMPLE 3 · A CIRCUMCIRCLE IN THE COORDINATE SYSTEM

Construct the circumcircle of the triangle with $A(1, 1)$, $B(7, 1)$ and $C(3, 5)$. One unit is 1 cm.

The perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$ is the perpendicular through the midpoint $(4, 1)$. Construct the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AC}$ with compasses.

The two intersect at $U(4, 2)$. Check: the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{BC}$ also passes through $U$.

The circumcircle with centre $U(4, 2)$ has the radius $r \approx 3.2$ cm (measured).

EXAMPLE 4 · A ROUND FLOWER BED

A triangular garden has a right angle; the sides next to it are 6 m and 8 m long. A round flower bed is to be as large as possible. Draw it to the scale 1 : 100.

The largest bed is the incircle. Construct two angle bisectors; their point of intersection is $I$. Drop the perpendicular from $I$ to one side.

In the drawing you measure $\varrho = 2$ cm. The bed has a radius of 2 m.

EXERCISES

Draw an acute-angled triangle. Construct the circumcircle and the incircle. Check with compasses whether the circumcircle really passes through all the corners.

Two perpendicular bisectors give $U$, two angle bisectors give $I$. Both points lie inside. Drawn accurately, the circle with centre $U$ meets all three corners.

Where is the circumcentre? a) $\alpha = 50^\circ$, $\beta = 60^\circ$   b) $\alpha = 30^\circ$, $\beta = 60^\circ$   c) $\alpha = 25^\circ$, $\beta = 40^\circ$

a) $\gamma = 70^\circ$, acute-angled: inside   b) $\gamma = 90^\circ$: at the midpoint of the hypotenuse $\overline{AB}$   c) $\gamma = 115^\circ$, obtuse-angled: outside

Three villages want a shared radio mast that is the same distance from all three villages. How do you find the place? What if the villages lie almost on one line?

The place is the circumcentre. If the villages lie almost on one line, the triangle is very obtuse: $U$ lies far outside, and the mast would be far away from all the villages.

Show that in an equilateral triangle $U$ and $I$ coincide.

In an equilateral triangle the perpendicular bisector of a side passes through the opposite corner and bisects the angle there. So it is also an angle bisector. The three lines are the same, and so is their point of intersection.

Explain why the three angle bisectors of a triangle intersect in one point.

The point of intersection $I$ of the angle bisectors at $A$ and $B$ is the same distance from $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ (angle bisector at $A$) and from $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BC}$ (at $B$). So it is also the same distance from $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{BC}$ and lies on the angle bisector at $C$.

TEST YOURSELF!

A right-angled triangle has a hypotenuse 10 cm long. What is the radius of its circumcircle?

$U$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse: $r = 5$ cm.

A triangle has $\alpha = 40^\circ$ and $\beta = 45^\circ$. Where is $U$?

$\gamma = 95^\circ$: obtuse-angled, $U$ lies outside.

What is the smallest number of angle bisectors you have to construct to find $I$?

Two. The third passes through their point of intersection by itself.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A circle has the centre $M(4, 4)$ and the radius 3. How do the lines $y = 1$, $y = 0$ and $x = 6$ lie?

$y = 1$: distance 3, tangent. $y = 0$: distance 4, external line. $x = 6$: distance 2, secant.

The triangle $A(0, 0)$, $B(8, 0)$, $C(0, 6)$ has a right angle at $A$. Where is $U$? Measure $\overline{BC}$ and give the radius of the circumcircle.

$U$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $\overline{BC}$: $U(4, 3)$. You measure $\overline{BC} = 10$, so $r = 5$.

Connecting with Year 6: In a triangle $\gamma = 90^\circ$ and $\alpha$ is twice as big as $\beta$. Calculate the angles. Where is $U$?

$\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$ and $\alpha = 2\beta$, so $3\beta = 90^\circ$: $\beta = 30^\circ$, $\alpha = 60^\circ$. $U$ lies at the midpoint of the hypotenuse $\overline{AB}$.

A circle has $r = 2$ cm; a point $P$ is 5 cm from $M$. Draw as accurately as possible all the lines through $P$ that touch the circle. How many do you find? (In chapter 1.3 you learn how to construct them exactly.)

There are exactly two tangents through $P$, symmetrical about the line $MP$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Euclid and the two circles

Around 300 BC Euclid wrote the Elements in Alexandria, thirteen books on geometry and numbers. For more than 2000 years, pupils in Europe learned geometry from this work. Many of the theorems you get to know this school year are already in it.

In the fourth book Euclid shows how to inscribe a circle in a triangle (Proposition 4) and how to draw a circle round a triangle (Proposition 5). He proceeds exactly as you do: for the incircle he bisects two angles, for the circumcircle he erects the perpendiculars at the midpoints of two sides. And he already notes that the centre of the circumcircle lies inside, on a side or outside, depending on whether the opposite angle is acute, right or obtuse.

Sources: Euclid, Elements, Book IV, Propositions 4 and 5 with corollary. English translation with figures: D. E. Joyce, Clark University.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

CIRCLE AND LINE

$d > r$ external line · $d = r$ tangent · $d < r$ secant

$r = 3$ cm, $d = 2$ cm: secant

TANGENT

Perpendicular to the radius $\overline{MB}$ at the point of contact $B$.

Construction: perpendicular to $MB$ at $B$

CIRCUMCIRCLE

Point of intersection $U$ of the perpendicular bisectors, the same distance from all corners

inside · midpoint of the hypotenuse · outside

INCIRCLE

Point of intersection $I$ of the angle bisectors, the same distance from all sides

$I$ always lies inside

TESTTWO ROUNDS · INSTANT FEEDBACK
ROUND 1 · IN YOUR HEAD

$r = 6$ cm, $d = 6$ cm: how many points do the circle and the line have in common?

Tangent: exactly one.

A triangle has $\alpha = 30^\circ$ and $\beta = 50^\circ$. How big is $\gamma$?

$180^\circ - 30^\circ - 50^\circ = 100^\circ$. So the circumcentre lies outside.

A right-angled triangle has a hypotenuse 13 cm long. What is the radius of the circumcircle?

$13 \div 2 = 6.5$ cm

ROUND 2 · THINKING IT THROUGH

A circle has a diameter of 9 cm. A line is 4 cm from the centre. How many points do they have in common?

$r = 4.5$ cm $> 4$ cm: secant, two points.

Where is the incentre of an obtuse-angled triangle?

The incentre always lies inside.

At what angle does the tangent meet the radius to the point of contact?

At a right angle: 90°.
